{{Short description|1986 Japanese animated film by Hayao Miyazaki}} {{About|the 1986 animated film||Castles in the Sky (disambiguation)}} {{good article}} {{Use shortened footnotes|date=February 2026}} {{Use American English |date=June 2023}} {{Use mdy dates|date=January 2024}} {{Infobox film | name = Castle in the Sky | native_name = {{Infobox Japanese | japanese = 天空の城ラピュタ | revhep = Tenkū no Shiro Rapyuta}} | image = Castle in the Sky (1986).png | alt = The poster for Castle in the Sky, depicting Sheeta, her glowing necklace, and Pazu ready to catch her upon a ledge | caption = Theatrical release poster | director = [[Hayao Miyazaki]] | writer = Hayao Miyazaki | starring = {{ubl|[[Mayumi Tanaka]]|[[Keiko Yokozawa]]|{{ill|lt=Kotoe Hatsui|初井言榮|ja}}|[[Minori Terada]]}} | music = [[Joe Hisaishi]] | producer = [[Isao Takahata]] | editing = {{ubl|[[Takeshi Seyama]]|Yoshihiro Kasahara}} | cinematography = Hirokata Takahashi | studio = [[Studio Ghibli]] | distributor = [[Toei Company]] | released = {{Film date|1986|8|2}} | runtime = 124 minutes | country = Japan | language = Japanese }} '''''Castle in the Sky''''', also known as {{Nihongo foot|'''''Laputa: Castle in the Sky'''''|天空の城ラピュタ|Tenkū no Shiro Rapyuta|post=,|lead=yes|group=lower-alpha}} is a 1986 Japanese [[Anime|animated]] [[Fantasy film|fantasy]] [[adventure film]] written and directed by [[Hayao Miyazaki]]. It was produced by [[Isao Takahata]], animated by [[Studio Ghibli]], and distributed by the [[Toei Company]]. The film stars the voices of [[Mayumi Tanaka]], [[Keiko Yokozawa]], {{ill|lt=Kotoe Hatsui|初井言榮|ja}}, and [[Minori Terada]]. In the film, orphans Sheeta and Pazu are pursued by government agent Muska, the army, and a group of pirates. They seek Sheeta's crystal necklace, the key to accessing Laputa, a legendary flying castle hosting advanced technology. ''Castle in the Sky'' was the first film to be animated by Studio Ghibli. Its production team included many of Miyazaki's longtime collaborators, who would continue to work with the studio for the following three decades. The film was partly inspired by Miyazaki's trips to Wales, where he witnessed the aftermath of the [[1984–1985 United Kingdom miners' strike|1984–1985 coal miners' strike]]. The island of Laputa is used to highlight the theme of environmentalism, exploring the relationships between humanity, nature, and technology, a reflection of Miyazaki's ecological philosophy. The young protagonists also provide a unique perspective on the narrative, as a result of Miyazaki's desire to portray "the honesty and goodness of children in [his] work".{{harvnb|Miyazaki|2009|p=50}}, cited in {{harvnb|Napier|2018|p=93}}. Many aspects of the film's [[retrofuturistic]] style – the flying machines in particular – are influenced by nineteenth-century approaches, which has earned the film a reputation in the modern [[steampunk]] genre. The film was released in Japanese theaters on August 2, 1986. It underperformed expectations at the box office, but later achieved commercial success through rereleases. An English dub commissioned by [[Tokuma Shoten]] was distributed in North America by [[Streamline Pictures]], and another dub was produced by [[Walt Disney Pictures|Disney]] in 1998, released internationally by [[Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment|Buena Vista]] in 2003. The film's score was composed by [[Joe Hisaishi]], who would become a close collaborator of Miyazaki's; Hisaishi also composed a reworked soundtrack for the 2003 English dub. The film was generally acclaimed by critics, though the English dubs received mixed reviews. It was well received by audiences, being voted as one of the [[List of films considered the best|greatest animated films]] in polls conducted by the [[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] and [[Oricon]]. The film also received several notable accolades, including the [[Ōfuji Noburō Award]] at the [[Mainichi Film Awards]] and the [[Anime Grand Prix]] from ''Animage''. ''Castle in the Sky'' has since attained [[cult film|cult status]],{{sfn|McCarthy|2002|p=97}} and has influenced several notable artists working in multiple media. == Plot summary == An airship carrying Sheeta{{nbsp}}– an orphan girl abducted by the government agent Muska{{nbsp}}– is attacked by Dola and her air pirate gang, who seek Sheeta's crystal necklace. Attempting to escape, Sheeta falls from the airship but is saved by the crystal's magic, which gently lowers her to the ground. Pazu, an orphan working as a mechanic in a 19th-century mining town, catches her and takes her home to recover. The following morning, he shows Sheeta a photograph his father took of Laputa, a mythical castle on a flying island that Pazu hopes to find. Soon afterward, Dola's gang and Muska's soldiers arrive searching for Sheeta. Fleeing through the town, Pazu and Sheeta fall into a mine shaft, where the crystal again saves them. In the tunnels, they meet Uncle Pom, who reveals deposits of the glowing mineral Aetherium, the same material as Sheeta's crystal. Sheeta reveals to Pazu her secret name that ties her to Laputa, confirming the legend is real. The army captures the pair and imprisons them in Titus Fort, where Muska shows Sheeta a deactivated robot bearing the same insignia as her crystal and reveals she is heir to the Laputan throne. He releases Pazu in exchange for Sheeta's cooperation in locating Laputa. Returning home, Pazu is captured by Dola's gang, who intend to steal the crystal from Titus Fort. He joins them in an attempt to rescue Sheeta. At the fort, Sheeta recites an ancient phrase taught by her grandmother, inadvertently activating the crystal's power and reanimating the robot. The robot protects her from the soldiers and devastates the fort before being destroyed by the military airship ''Goliath''. Amid the chaos, Pazu and Dola rescue Sheeta, but Muska retains the crystal, whose magic guides him toward Laputa. Using clues she observed from the crystal, Sheeta helps Pazu persuade Dola to take them to Laputa in exchange for temporarily joining her crew. During the journey, ''Goliath'' attacks Dola's airship. Dola detaches the crow's nest{{nbsp}}– containing Sheeta and Pazu{{nbsp}}– which functions as a glider tethered to the ship, while Pazu identifies a massive storm where he believes Laputa is hidden. Violent winds destroy the airship and sever the glider's tether, sending Pazu and Sheeta through the storm. They arrive safely on Laputa, finding it largely deserted except for wildlife and a peaceful robot caretaker. The castle lies in ruins beneath a giant tree growing from the island's center. The army soon arrives and begins looting the castle after capturing Dola's gang. Muska betrays the soldiers, destroys their communications equipment, and takes Sheeta into the castle's core, which houses Laputa's ancient knowledge and weaponry. Using the crystal, he activates the city's defenses and reveals that he, too, descends from the Laputan royal line. After demonstrating Laputa's power by causing a massive explosion over the ocean and destroying ''Goliath'', Muska declares his intention to use the city to dominate humanity. Horrified, Sheeta steals back the crystal and flees, but Muska corners her in Laputa's throne room. Pazu arrives and negotiates a brief truce, allowing Sheeta to teach him the spell of destruction. Together, they recite it, causing Muska to fall to his death as Laputa collapses around them. The giant tree shields Sheeta and Pazu from the destruction and preserves part of the castle, along with Dola's glider, as the island rises into space. Sheeta, Pazu, and Dola's gang escape safely and briefly reunite before parting ways. == Voice cast == {{Multiple image | align = right | direction = vertical | width = 150 | image1 = Mayumi Tanaka 2023.jpg | caption1 = [[Mayumi Tanaka]] ''(pictured in 2023)'', who voiced Pazu in the original Japanese{{sfn|''Nausicaa.net''}} | alt1 = Mayumi Tanaka holding a microphone and smiling | image2 = Mark Hamill (2017).jpg | caption2 = [[Mark Hamill]] ''(2017)'', who played Muska in the 2003 English dub{{sfn|''Nausicaa.net''}} | alt2 = A portrait of Mark Hamill }} {{Plain row headers}} {| class="wikitable plain-row-headers" ! scope="colgroup" colspan="2" |Character name ! scope="colgroup" colspan="3" |Voice actor{{sfn|''Nausicaa.net''}} |- ! scope="col" width="20%" rowspan="2" | English ! scope="col" width="20%" rowspan="2" | Japanese ! scope="col" width="20%" rowspan="2" | Japanese

Miller]] |} == Development == === Early concepts === Following the success of his previous film, ''[[Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (film)|Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind]]''{{nbsp}}(1984), [[Hayao Miyazaki]] began looking for different projects to direct.{{sfnm|Napier|2018|1p=86|2a1=Odell|2a2=Le Blanc|2y=2015|2p=64}} [[Tokuma Shoten]], the company backing Miyazaki financially, proposed producing a follow-up to ''Nausicaä'', which he refused.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|1p=76|2a1=Odell|2a2=Le Blanc|2y=2015|2p=64}} He envisioned creating an old-fashioned adventure film that would be a "pleasure" to watch,{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=86}} for which he took a research trip to the city of [[Yanagawa, Fukuoka|Yanagawa]]. He developed an initial film concept set in the city, tentatively titled ''Blue Mountains'',{{sfn|Miyazaki|2016|pp=8–9}}{{efn|[[Seiji Kanō]] reported the title of this concept was {{nihongo|''The City Where the Water Flows''|水の流れる街|Mizu no nagareru machi|lead=yes}}.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=76}}}} which he pitched to Tokuma Shoten in June{{nbsp}}1984.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=76}} However, he stated in a later interview that he "wasn't in shape to direct" at the time, and was unable to make progress on the concept.{{harvnb|Nomura|1986|p=46}}, cited in {{harvnb|Denison|2018|p=35}}. [[File:Yanagawa-kawakudari.jpg|thumb|upright=0.9|Research for an abandoned concept set in [[Yanagawa, Fukuoka|Yanagawa]] inspired [[Isao Takahata]] to create a documentary focusing on the city's canals instead.{{sfn|Odell|Le Blanc|2015|pp=68–69}}|alt=Boats flow down a canal between houses.]] The film was never produced, but the city's canals inspired Miyazaki's longtime collaborator, [[Isao Takahata]], to propose they create a documentary about them rather than an animation. This eventually became ''[[The Story of Yanagawa's Canals]]''{{nbsp}}(1987), which focused on the environmental effects of industry on the local waterways.{{sfn|Odell|Le Blanc|2015|pp=68–69}} A documentary, however, was unlikely to be commercially viable and had no prospect of support from Tokuma Shoten.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|1pp=76–77|2a1=Odell|2a2=Le Blanc|2y=2015|2p=68}} Miyazaki therefore financed its production through his personal office, Nibariki, using the profits he had made from ''Nausicaä''.{{sfn|Denison|2018|p=35}} Takahata rapidly spent the funds on research;{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=77}} to recover the expense and help complete the filming, [[Toshio Suzuki]], an editor of ''[[Animage]]'' at the time, recommended that Miyazaki direct another film.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=77}} According to Suzuki, Miyazaki immediately agreed,{{sfn|Stimson|2014}} and quickly developed a concept for the film based on an idea he had in elementary school.{{harvnb|Miyazaki|2002|p=280}}, cited in {{harvnb|Kawakatsu|2010|p=95}}.{{efn|The lead characters' names date back to this story; ''Pazu'' is an original name, while ''Sheeta'' is derived from the Greek letter [[theta]].{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|2022|p=29}}}} Suzuki later commented that "if Takahata had made his movie on schedule, [''Castle in the Sky''] wouldn't have been born."{{sfn|Stimson|2014}} === Pre-production === Miyazaki completed a project proposal in December{{nbsp}}1984, tentatively titled ''Young Boy Pazu''.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|1p=77|Napier|2018|2p=86}}{{efn|[[Japanese language|Japanese]]: {{lang|ja|少年パズー}}, [[Hepburn romanization|Hepburn]]: {{tlit|ja|Hepburn|Shōnen Pazū}}. A few other titles were suggested in the proposal, including ''Mystery of the Levitation Crystal'' and ''Flying Treasure Island''.{{sfn|Miyazaki|2009|p=252}}}} According to the animation scholar [[Seiji Kanō]], its concepts constituted a "direct rebellion" against popular animation trends at the time; instead of a protagonist with superhuman powers and a futuristic setting, the proposal featured an ordinary child within a fantastical nineteenth-century period.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|1p=78|Napier|2018|2pp=87–88}} Although Miyazaki had expected ''Nausicaä'' to appeal to teenagers, he realized that his audience also included many younger children. This led him to conceptualize a film catered to this demographic, opposed to the trend of increasingly [[Adult animation|adult-oriented animations]].{{sfn|Kanō|2006|pp=76–77}} The proposal was also unusual in that it did not adapt an already-successful [[manga]], which weakened its commercial potential.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|1p=78|Napier|2018|2p=92}} Feeling that it was unlikely to be green-lit, Miyazaki preemptively began work on a back-up proposal. However, Tokuma Shoten was eager to back ''Young Boy Pazu'',{{sfn|Yoshioka|2018|p=19}} and immediately approved it to begin production, with Takahata acting as producer as he had done on ''Nausicaä''.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=78}} Miyazaki continued working on the proposal, producing a second draft in February{{nbsp}}1985. Kanō wrote that this one contained a shift towards a more realistic perspective; refinements were made to the plot, multiple settings were described in detail, and additional characters were included.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=78}} {{Multiple image | align = right | direction = vertical | width = 200 | image1 = Cardiff Castle - 2022-08-18 (18).jpg | alt1 = An ancient stone castle | image2 = Big Pit National Coal Museum, Blaenavon, Wales June 12, 2015 (49526156446).jpg | alt2 = A collection of brick-and-mortar structures on a grassy hillside | footer = [[Cardiff Castle]] ''(top)'' and [[Big Pit National Coal Museum|Big Pit Mine]] ''(bottom)'' in southern Wales, where Miyazaki visited during his [[location scouting]] trip{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=78}} }} Miyazaki had previously visited the country of Wales in 1984, where he witnessed the [[1984–1985 United Kingdom miners' strike|1984–1985 coal miners' strike]] in protest of the push from [[Margaret Thatcher]]'s government to close many of the mines.{{sfnm|1a1=Brooks|1y=2005|2a1=Odell|2a2=Le Blanc|2y=2015|2p=64}} On Takahata's suggestion, Miyazaki traveled there again in May{{nbsp}}1985 to conduct [[location scouting]] for the film. With Takahata and Suzuki occupied with the documentary and with building the film's production crew, Miyazaki went alone.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|1p=78|Napier|2018|2p=90}} Although using real locations as inspirations for fictional settings was a common practice among Japanese animators,{{sfn|Denison|2020|p=69}} Miyazaki's intention for the film was only a generally Western appearance.{{harvnb|Takahata|1991|p=296}}, cited in {{harvnb|Lamarre|2009|p=327|loc=note 1}}. He was significantly influenced by the region's architecture and landscapes;{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=90}} the [[Big Pit National Coal Museum|Big Pit Mine]]{{nbsp}}– by then converted into a museum{{nbsp}}– influenced the opening scenes set in the mining village. [[Cardiff Castle]], and other edifices like it around Wales, provided references for the film's Titus Fort.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=78}} He was moved by the empty facilities and defeated atmosphere of the miners he witnessed, which resonated with him politically and influenced the themes that he eventually explored.{{sfn|Napier|2018|pp=90–91}}{{efn|See {{slink|#Working-class moralities}} for further information.}} === Writing and production === {{Multiple image | align = right | direction = vertical | width = 150 | image1 = HayaoMiyazakiCCJuly09.jpg | caption1 = [[Hayao Miyazaki]] ''(pictured in 2009)'', the writer and director | image2 = Isao Takahata (cropped).jpg | caption2 = [[Isao Takahata]] ''(2014)'', the producer }} While Miyazaki was away, Takahata, Suzuki, and Tokuma Shoten's {{ill|Yasuyoshi Tokuma|ja|徳間康快}} searched for an animation studio willing to take on the new production, but were unsuccessful. The company responsible for ''Nausicaä''{{'s}} production, [[Topcraft]], had also gone bankrupt around the time. They therefore decided to set up a new studio, hiring some of their previous collaborators, including {{ill|Tōru Hara (producer)|lt=Tōru Hara|ja|原徹}}{{nbsp}}– Topcraft's founder{{nbsp}}– and the colorist [[Michiyo Yasuda]].{{sfnm|Denison|2018|1p=34|Denison|2023|2p=42}} After scouting several properties on which to set up an office, they selected a location in Tokyo's [[Kichijōji]] neighborhood, and were set to begin production upon Miyazaki's return. [[Studio Ghibli]] opened on June{{nbsp}}15, 1985, as a subsidiary of Tokuma Shoten.{{sfnm|Denison|2023|1p=39|Kanō|2006|2p=79}}{{efn|The circumstances surrounding the formation of [[Studio Ghibli]] are the subject of debate among animation scholars. See {{harvnb|Denison|2018}} and {{harvnb|Denison|2023}} for further information.}} Along with some initial sketches of the visuals, Miyazaki began working on the script on June{{nbsp}}17, the first draft of which was completed by the end of the month.{{sfn|Kameyama|2016|p=11}} The film's title, ''Laputa: Castle in the Sky'', was finalized.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|pp=79–80}} This draft's plot was similar to that of the finished film until the substantially different final act: Sheeta and Pazu remained separated throughout their time on Laputa, more scenes of violence and strife that occur there were included, and additional runtime was spent on an exploration of Muska's character. Takahata and Suzuki, who felt that this deviated from the intended adventurous mood, advised Miyazaki to make revisions.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=81}} A second script draft was finished on July{{nbsp}}22. In addition to changes to the second half of the plot, new elements began to appear: the power of Sheeta's necklace became tied to her thoughts, and Laputa's natural elements were emphasized.{{sfn|Kameyama|2016|p=11}} However, other concepts that had featured in Miyazaki's concept art for several years, such as a scene in which Sheeta and Pazu pilot an [[ornithopter]], were cut. Miyazaki also began the [[storyboarding]] around this time.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=81}} Studio Ghibli gradually built its production staff over the following months and began work on the main animation,{{sfn|Kameyama|2016|pp=11–12}} recruiting animators from companies they had previously worked with, such as [[Telecom Animation Film]], [[Toei Animation]], and [[Nippon Animation]].{{sfnm|Denison|2023|1p=46|Kanō|2006|2p=82}} The [[key animation]] was done by a team of 21,{{sfn|Denison|2023|p=62}} and other studios, such as [[Doga Kobo]] and [[Oh! Production]], provided support for the [[in-between animation]].{{sfn|''Nausicaa.net''}} Unusually for the industry, two art directors were assigned to create the backgrounds; these were made with [[watercolors]] or other kinds of paint on paper.{{sfn|Denison|2023|pp=61–62}} By January{{nbsp}}1986, 33{{nbsp}}people were working on the project in total. Filming of completed sequences began the following month, and a teaser trailer was sent out to theaters. Miyazaki finalized the storyboards; according to Kanō, they required significant condensing, as the original plan would have run over three hours. The final runtime was just over two hours, making it Miyazaki's longest film at the time.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=82}} === Animation and special effects === ''Castle in the Sky'' was [[Traditional animation|animated by hand]] using at least 69,262{{nbsp}}[[cel]] drawings.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|1p=74|Lamarre|2002|2p=341}}{{efn|Some sources claimed that the film uses as many as 75,000{{nbsp}}cels.{{sfnm|Kameyama|2016|1p=12|Kothenschulte|2021|2p=61}}}} Hara said that the studio was "aiming for a manga-like feel", which they planned to accomplish with a limited color palette. However, they ended up using over 300{{nbsp}}shades, which Yasuda attributed to the varied lighting conditions across the film;{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|1986|p=156}} by comparison, ''Nausicaä'' had used only around{{nbsp}}250.{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|1986|p=157}} The lead animator [[Yoshinori Kanada]] was hired in August{{nbsp}}1985,{{sfn|Kameyama|2016|p=11}} and the first task he was delegated was to experiment on the flaptors{{nbsp}}– the flying machines used by Dola's gang in the film. He attempted multiple approaches to portray their insect-like wings, eventually deciding upon [[drybrush]]ed strokes to imply rapid motion.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|1p=94|Miyazaki|2016|2p=110}} Certain special effects from the film use a combination of cel and film techniques.{{sfn|Miyazaki|2016|p=36}} For example, [[double exposure]]s in which parts of the image are exposed only once, creating the effect of semi-transparency; this technique was used in the film to depict Laputa's holograms.{{sfnm|Denison|2023|1p=102|Miyazaki|2016|2p=158}} The opening sequence uses multiple "transmitted light" techniques{{nbsp}}– in which the film is deliberately overexposed, allowing light to bleed into adjacent sections of the image{{nbsp}}– to convey the luminance of the crystal necklace.{{sfn|Miyazaki|2016|p=36}} According to Hara, the majority of the cels had been completed by May{{nbsp}}1986, but around 30% required retouching during the filming process.{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|1986|p=157}} Some of the film's shots make use of the Harmony Process, a technique pioneered by {{ill|Noriko Takaya (animator)|lt=Noriko Takaya|ja|高屋法子}}.{{harvnb|Studio Ghibli|1986|p=93}}, cited in {{harvnb|Denison|2023|p=104}}. This involved cutting cels into custom shapes and painting them in the style of a background layer, which could then be moved between frames in a manner comparable to [[stop-motion animation]]. This allowed certain foreground elements to be highly detailed as, unlike the other cels, they did not have to be redrawn on every frame.{{sfn|Denison|2023|pp=103–104}} An early shot of the ''Goliath'' airship that Takaya worked on features Harmony elements,{{sfnm|Denison|2023|1p=105|Studio Ghibli|1986|2p=93}} and a similar technique was used to animate the storm initially obscuring Laputa.{{sfn|Miyazaki|2016|p=143}} === Casting and voice acting === Auditions for the voice cast began in May{{nbsp}}1986,{{sfn|Kameyama|2016|p=12}} led by Miyazaki, Takahata, and [[Shigeharu Shiba]], the film's sound director. Pazu was initially intended to be voiced by a young boy, but they found the audition performances unsatisfactory. Shiba eventually recommended [[Mayumi Tanaka]], who was known for other voice roles playing children. For Sheeta, Miyazaki requested they cast someone other than [[Sumi Shimamoto]], who had voiced the female leads of his two previous films; they finally decided on [[Keiko Yokozawa]], a veteran voice actor who had also tried out for the lead role in ''Nausicaä''.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=97}} [[Minori Terada]] (Muska) and {{ill|Kotoe Hatsui|ja|初井言榮}} (Dola) were considered unusual choices, as they were both known more for their careers in live-action films. Shiba stated that Terada was selected in part due to his voice's similarity to the actor [[Jinpachi Nezu]]'s, but that he and Miyazaki had also been impressed by Terada's work on the Japanese dub of ''[[Blade Runner]]''{{nbsp}}(1982).{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|1986|p=163}} Shiba considered casting a comedian from the [[Kansai region]] as Dola, but Miyazaki found [[Kansai dialect|their dialect of Japanese]] to be undesirable. However, after he happened to view a television program in which Hatsui talked about her past, Shiba was impressed by her voice and personality, and handed her the role.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=97}} The voice recordings took place over three days in late June and early July.{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|1986|pp=158–162}} As further changes had been made to the story since the last script draft, the scripts given to the voice actors consisted of dialog extracted from the storyboards.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=81}} Terada, who was voicing an animated character for the first time, initially had difficulty delivering his lines in sync with Muska's lip movements; however, he grasped the technique during rehearsals and, according to Shiba, made a confident performance.{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|1986|p=163}} == Themes == === Roles of nature and technology === ''Castle in the Sky'' contains a strong theme of [[environmentalism]], questioning humanity's relationship with nature and the role of technology.{{sfn|Odell|Le Blanc|2015|pp=23–24}} McCarthy interprets the giant tree of Laputa as a "metaphor for the reviving and life-giving power of nature."{{sfn|McCarthy|2002|p=98}} However, in contrast with the more optimistic conclusions of Miyazaki's previous works, Napier notes that the film ends with an "unsettling view" of the castle flying away, suggesting that humanity may not deserve to exist in the natural world.{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=94}} Literary scholar Anthony Lioi interprets Laputa as an ecological [[utopia]] that demonstrates the peace that can be established between nature and advanced technology, but also serves as a criticism of modernity when "[the] peace is shattered by human violence."{{sfn|Lioi|2010}} Lioi notes that this outlook differs from dominant Western ideas, eschewing the extremes of [[capitalism]] and [[industrialism]], as well as radical environmentalism and [[conservationism]].{{sfn|Lioi|2010}} [[File:Laputa Castle in the Sky, screencap 2.jpg |thumb|While Laputa's giant tree is seen as a metaphor for the restorative capability of the natural world, its underside is a symbol of the immorality of modernity.{{sfn|Lioi|2010}} |alt=The flying castle Laputa, with the giant tree on top and weapons system underneath]] Critics note the philosophical ambiguity of the castle; while Laputa initially appears to be an ideal union of nature and technology, it is later revealed to have a much harsher and more oppressive underside;{{sfn|McCarthy|2002|p=98}} Napier writes that Laputa is "deeply paradoxical".{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=98}} Laputa itself takes direct inspiration from the [[Laputa|island of the same name]] from ''[[Gulliver's Travels]]'' (1726),{{sfnm|1a1=Miyazaki|1y=2009|1p=252|2a1=Napier|2y=2018|2p=88}} and film scholar Cristina Cardia claims that, like its namesake, the island is introduced with benign intentions but is ultimately "exploited for perverse ends, in this case war."{{sfn|Cardia|2018|p=14}} Lioi argues that Laputa is used as a means to comment on the ethics of contemporary culture,{{sfn|Lioi|2010}} based on Ildney Cavalcanti's observation that such a utopia also "must contain an overtly dystopian element, such that the implicit critique in utopian discourse becomes explicit."{{harvnb|Cavalcanti|2004|p=48}}, cited in {{harvnb|Lioi|2010}}. However, he interprets the ultimate destruction of the castle's weapons as a demonstration that "violence is not the heart of the city", and that the dystopic elements of modernity can be healed.{{sfn|Lioi|2010}} The film also presents an ambiguous view on the usage of technology.{{sfn|Odell|Le Blanc|2015|p=26}} The robots from Laputa provide an example of this view, as they are introduced in the film as a violent force capable of extreme destruction. However, when the protagonists next meet a robot, it is entirely peaceful, tending to the gardens and fauna on Laputa.{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=95}} Lioi argues that the robots, as a representation of Laputan technology, are caretakers by default and only become destructive in response to human brutality.{{sfn|Lioi|2010}} McCarthy argues that "this is not a comment on technology but on man's inability to use it wisely."{{sfn|McCarthy|2002|p=95}} Odell and Le Blanc conclude that "technology{{nbsp}}... is not necessarily a bad thing, but we must consider how it's used and to what extent."{{sfn|Odell|Le Blanc|2015|p=24}} The duality of nature and technology is further explored in Miyazaki's later film ''[[Princess Mononoke]]'' (1997).{{sfn|Odell|Le Blanc|2015|p=25}} === Innocence of children === Like many other films by Miyazaki, ''Castle in the Sky'' features young children as protagonists.{{sfn|Odell|Le Blanc|2015|p=26}} Miyazaki values the portrayal of children as good-hearted, confident in their own agency, and resilient and upbeat in response to adversity.{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=92}} He criticized reviewers of his television series ''[[Future Boy Conan]]'' (1978) who described the titular character as "too much of a goody-two-shoes", admitting he was tempted to retort "So you want to see 'bad characters', you fool?"{{harvnb|Miyazaki|2009|p=295}}, cited in {{harvnb|Napier|2018|p=92}}. Film critics [[Colin Odell and Michelle Le Blanc]] argue that creating a film with younger protagonists generates perspectives that an adult would not perceive, saying "the children in Ghibli's films are a liberating force that allows anything to be possible."{{sfn|Odell|Le Blanc|2015|p=26}} The lack of parental oversight of the protagonists is an element Miyazaki feels to be important in promoting children's independence. The protagonists of his films are, like Sheeta and Pazu, often orphaned, or in some way parted from their parents.{{sfn|Napier|2018|pp=92–93}} Miyazaki believes that "one of the essential elements of most classical children's literature is that the children in the stories actually fend for themselves."{{harvnb|Miyazaki|2009|p=341}}, cited in {{harvnb|Napier|2018|p=92}}. The presence of parents, in his opinion, would stifle the children's autonomy.{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=93}} The limitations that children have in their abilities are also explored in the film; for example, Pazu comes close to forsaking Sheeta and his quest for Laputa.{{sfn|Greenberg|2018|p=111}} Additionally, unlike Miyazaki's previous works, the protagonists do not succeed at convincing the antagonists of their wrongdoing, which offers a more pessimistic view on children's ability to educate others.{{sfn|Greenberg|2018|p=111}} Napier proposes that Miyazaki's insistence on showing the freedom of children in ''Castle in the Sky'' can be credited to the influence of ''[[Panda and the Magic Serpent]]'' (1958).{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=93}} Miyazaki first watched the film at age 17, and it moved him to pursue a career in animation.{{sfn|Greenberg|2018|p=4}} At a lecture given in 1982 at [[Waseda University]], he said "When I saw ''Panda and the Magic Serpent'', it was as if the scales fell from my eyes; I realized that I should depict the honesty and goodness of children in my work." He considers this a focal point in his endeavors. The theme of innocence is explored further in Miyazaki's succeeding film ''[[My Neighbor Totoro]]'' (1988).{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=105}} === Working-class moralities === While in Wales for his location scouting, Miyazaki witnessed the aftermath of the 1984–1985 coal miners' strike. Their ultimate failure to preserve the industry left a lasting impact on him; he viewed the event as an attack by the powerful on the miners' way of life and hard-working spirit.{{sfn|Greenberg|2018|p=110}} His experiences are reflected in several supporting characters in the film, who, despite living impoverished lives of hard labor in the mines, enthusiastically protect the protagonists from multiple aggressors. Napier argued that this depiction reveals Miyazaki's yearning for a simpler way of life and a desire to create a story based in optimism.{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=91}} Miyazaki later stated that he had "felt a real sense of solidarity with the mine workers" while in Wales;{{sfn|Miyazaki|2009|p=339}} Kanō speculated that they reminded him of his time in a [[labor union]] while working at Toei Animation.{{harvnb|Kanō|2006|p=93}}, cited in {{harvnb|Napier|2018|p=90}}. The animation scholar [[Helen McCarthy]] wrote that the film "also contains echoes of the struggle of the Welsh people for nationhood and freedom."{{sfn|McCarthy|2002|p=96}} Miyazaki visited Wales once more in 1986, ahead of the release of the film. In 2005, he told ''[[The Guardian]]'' "I admired those men, I admired the way they battled to save their way of life, just as the coal miners in Japan did. Many people of my generation see the miners as a symbol, a dying breed of fighting men. Now they are gone."{{sfn|Brooks|2005}} == Style == === Combinations of prior work === Scholars have argued that ''Castle in the Sky'' represents an amalgamation of much of Miyazaki's prior work;{{sfnm|Denison|2018|Lamarre|2009|1p=37|2p=59}} the animation scholar [[Raz Greenberg]] felt that the film is "deeply rooted" within the previous twenty years of his career.{{sfn|Greenberg|2018|p=111}} On his creative process, Miyazaki said that "popular culture is characterized by repeated arrangements{{nbsp}}[...] what we want to inherit is what transcends time." Kanō noted that this "reconstructive approach" mirrored the compositional styles of classical writers. He saw this film as the meeting point of Miyazaki's "two opposing tendencies": the lighthearted cartoon tone he had established in works like ''The Castle of Cagliostro'' and ''Sherlock Hound'', and the serious exploration of modern themes in ''Nausicaä''.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=107}} Miyazaki stated that he based Sheeta in part on the character Hilda from ''[[The Great Adventure of Horus, Prince of the Sun]]''{{nbsp}}(1968), a Takahata-directed project he had contributed significantly to; both characters suffer hardship after inheriting powerful pendants.{{sfn|Lamarre|2009|p=57}} Lamarre found thematic parallels between the film and Miyazaki's series ''[[Future Boy Conan]]''{{nbsp}}(1978), including the post-apocalyptic setting and the protagonists' struggles to keep powerful men from deploying weapons of mass destruction.{{sfn|Lamarre|2009|p=58}} Some of the animals that appear on Laputa are references to Miyazaki's prior works. The robots are based on a similar character from ''[[Lupin the 3rd Part I]]''{{nbsp}}(1971–1972){{nbsp}}– a series Miyazaki and Takahata had partly directed{{nbsp}}– which was in turn inspired by ''[[The Mechanical Monsters]]''{{nbsp}}(1941), a [[Superman (1940s animated film series)|''Superman'' short film]] directed by [[Dave Fleischer]].{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=84}} Scenes from Miyazaki's manga ''[[Sabaku no Tami]]''{{nbsp}}(1969–1970) also bear resemblances to moments in the film.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=85}} === Literary influences === {{Multiple image | align = right | direction = vertical | width = 150 | image1 = Jules Verne by Étienne Carjat.jpg | image2 = Robert Louis Stevenson by Henry Walter Barnett bw.jpg | footer = The works of [[Jules Verne]] ''(pictured in 1884, top)'' and [[Robert Louis Stevenson]] ''(1893, bottom)'' were influential on the film's style.{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=89}} }} Miyazaki was stylistically inspired by the literature of [[Jules Verne]] and [[Robert Louis Stevenson]].{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=89}} Among Miyazaki's early intentions for the film was a revival of the classical adventure narrative in the manner of Stevenson's ''[[Treasure Island]]''{{nbsp}}(1883).{{harvnb|Kanō|2006|p=85}}; {{harvnb|Nomura|1986|p=43}}, cited in {{harvnb|Denison|2020|p=68}}. While at Toei Animation years prior, Miyazaki had worked on ''[[Animal Treasure Island]]''{{nbsp}}(1971), an adaptation of the novel. ''Treasure Island'' also became a primary influence on ''Castle in the Sky.''{{sfn|Napier|2017|p=77}} Many of the machines in the film are [[retrofuturistic]], influenced by nineteenth-century designs.{{sfnm|1a1=Lioi|1y=2010|2a1=Napier|2y=2018|2p=89}} The flying islands in the opening credits sequence are reminiscent of Verne's novel ''[[Propeller Island]]''{{nbsp}}(1895).{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=87}} In the film's proposal, Miyazaki expressed a desire to depict machines that "still possess the inherent warmth of handcrafted things."{{harvnb|Miyazaki|2009|p=254}}, cited in {{harvnb|Napier|2018|pp=89–90}}, and {{harvnb|VanderMeer|Chambers|2012|p=182}}. Influenced by Verne's style, the film envisions an alternative history featuring advanced technology, which scholars later analyzed as an example of [[steampunk]].{{sfnm|Napier|2018|Pearce|2021|1pp=89–90}} Commenting on the [[mecha anime]] popular at the time, Miyazaki expressed his hatred for shows that glorified machines without portraying the characters struggling to build or maintain them.{{sfn|Miyazaki|2009|p=20}} Kanō placed the film in opposition with [[cyberpunk]], writing that it attempts to "understand the present from the past", aligning with other steampunk works.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=107}} [[File:Pieter Bruegel the Elder - The Tower of Babel (Rotterdam) - Google Art Project - edited.jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.9|Among other sources, the design of Laputa was likely influenced by ''[[The Tower of Babel (Bruegel)|The Tower of Babel]]''{{nbsp}}({{circa|1563}}).{{sfn|Kanō|2006|pp=90–91}}|alt=Painting of an enormous structure along the water]] Studying early drawings for the film, Kanō argued that Miyazaki had likely incorporated elements of the [[Tower of Babel]], a mythical structure in the [[Book of Genesis]], when conceiving the island of Laputa. He found its design reminiscent of [[The Tower of Babel (Bruegel)|a painting of the tower]]{{nbsp}}({{circa|1563}}) by [[Pieter Bruegel the Elder]].{{sfn|Kanō|2006|pp=90–91}} Abeline also found [[Ancient Greek architecture|Ancient Greek]] and [[Architecture of Mesopotamia|Babylonian architectural]] influences.{{sfn|Abeline|2018|p=2}} In the scene where Muska deploys Laputa's weaponry, he claims it represents the [[Indrastra|arrow of Indra]] and was responsible for the destruction of the cities of [[Sodom and Gomorrah]], allusions to the ''[[Ramayana]]'' and the [[Old Testament]] respectively.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=88}} Miyazaki had previously been requested to adapt the ''Ramayana'' into an animated film, and although he declined the offer, he said that ideas he had encountered in his research{{nbsp}}– such as theories of the ancient Indians possessing nuclear weaponry{{nbsp}}– left an impression on him.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|pp=89–90}}{{efn|Miyazaki denied other parallels with the ''[[Ramayana]]'', however, such as the similarity between the names of ''Sheeta'' and ''[[Sita]]'', a character from the myth.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=90}}}} === Comparison with ''Gulliver's Travels'' === [[File:Wiki Loves Jules Verne Swift Gullivers Reisen Gelehrteninsel Laputa 1839 (Gerd Kueveler).jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.8|[[Laputa]], the flying island in ''[[Gulliver's Travels]]''{{nbsp}}(1726), was the namesake of the film's setting.|alt=Illustration of a person looking up at an island flying over a body of water]] The film's titular castle takes its name from [[Laputa]], the flying island from [[Jonathan Swift]]'s novel ''[[Gulliver's Travels]]''{{nbsp}}(1726).{{harvnb|Miyazaki|2009|p=253}}, cited in {{harvnb|Milthorpe|2025|p=205}}. ''Treasure Island'' provided Laputa's foundation in the narrative, but the idea that it would fly came from Swift.{{harvnb|''Asahi Shimbun''|1986}}, and {{harvnb|Nomura|1986|p=43}}, cited in {{harvnb|Denison|2018|pp=37–38}}. Miyazaki traced his connection with the novel to a library copy he had read in middle school; the literary scholar Brian Milthorpe proposed that he was referring to one of a series of abridged classics published by {{ill|Sogensha|ja|創元社}} for children.{{sfn|Milthorpe|2025|p=207}} He also recalled watching Fleischer's film [[Gulliver's Travels (1939 film)|''Gulliver's Travels'']]{{nbsp}}(1939) as a youth.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=91}} While at Toei, Miyazaki had worked as a key animator on ''[[Gulliver's Travels Beyond the Moon]]''{{nbsp}}(1965),{{sfn|Denison|2018|p=37}} a loose adaptation of Swift. Miyazaki had suggested an alternative ending in which a robot is unexpectedly revealed to be a human princess. The film's director, [[Yasuo Ōtsuka]], was impressed by this change and later spoke of it as an early example of Miyazaki's tendency toward humanist themes.{{sfn|Napier|2018|pp=36–37}} Miyazaki, however, dismissed the importance of the novel in interviews for ''Castle in the Sky'', saying that he included it in the film to sway potential sponsors{{harvnb|Nomura|1986|p=43}}, cited in {{harvnb|Denison|2018|p=38}}. and that he had "never read [it] in earnest even once."{{sfn|Milthorpe|2025|p=206}} Nevertheless, Milthorpe argued that Miyazaki's personal experience with the novel undergoes a "fictionalization". He found the narrative of Pazu's search for Laputa mirrored Miyazaki's process of adaptation; both seek the ideal of the island without engaging with the work in which it originated. In the film, Pazu dismisses Swift's tale as "just fantasy". Milthorpe analyzed this as a [[metalepsis]]; the film integrates another work of fiction into its diegesis, yet frames it as fictional within its internal logic.{{sfn|Milthorpe|2025|pp=206, 209–211}} Swift intended Laputa as a satire of the scientists of his time, particularly members of the [[Royal Society]], whose speculative theories he viewed as departures from common sense. The denizens of the island are depicted as completely disconnected from reality.{{sfn|Milthorpe|2025|pp=219–220}} The film does not take a satirical tone,{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=89}} but inherits Swift's style of presenting the fictional as real.{{sfn|Milthorpe|2025|pp=213, 215}} Sheeta and Pazu's exploration of Laputa parallels the [[wikt:travelogue|travelogue]] form of ''Gulliver's Travels'', according to Milthorpe,{{sfn|Milthorpe|2025|p=215}} and the islands in both works are suspended by great floating stones.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=91}} Swift's Laputa is also used as a weapon of mass destruction to exercise domination over the region underneath it; this aspect of the island critiqued [[the Crown]]'s use of power, particularly [[Ireland–United Kingdom relations#17th century|in Ireland]]. The desire to use the island as an instrument of political subjugation forms the basis of Muska's motivation in the film.{{sfn|Milthorpe|2025|pp=220–221}} Miyazaki's island, however, is an ambiguous symbol unlike its namesake.{{harvnb|Napier|2018|p=98}}, cited in {{harvnb|Milthorpe|2025|p=221}}.{{efn|See {{slink|#Roles of nature and technology}} for further information.}} Milthorpe analyzed it as a danger only due to Muska's refusal to acknowledge its nuances and relationships with fiction.{{sfn|Milthorpe|2025|pp=220–221}} == Release == === Marketing === To finance part of the production and the marketing campaign, Tokuma Shoten hired the advertising agency [[Dentsu]] to find [[tie-in]] sponsors, and they selected [[Toshiba]] and [[Ajinomoto]].{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|1p=102|Yoshioka|2018|2p=20}} An initial contract, which would have allowed them free use of film footage in commercials, was rejected by Takahata.{{sfn|Yoshioka|2018|p=20}} This decision was likely due to his lingering concerns about ''Nausicaä''{{'s}} campaign, where the studio had lost control over how their content was used.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|1p=102|Yoshioka|2018|2p=20}} The studio therefore allowed sponsors to use only concept sketches and the film's logo in promotional materials.{{harvnb|Suzuki|2005}}, cited in {{harvnb|Denison|2018|p=41}}; {{harvnb|Yoshioka|2018|p=20}}. While advertisements were run in several local newspapers,{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|2022|p=29}} and the ''[[Kinema Junpo]]'' magazine featured the film on the cover of its August{{nbsp}}1986 edition,{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|1996|p=123}} ''Animage''{{nbsp}}– Tokuma Shoten's specialist magazine{{nbsp}}– limited its promotional effort. While ''Nausicaä'' had been the subject of regular features and interviews, it published only an illustrated [[serial novel]] for this film. The magazine was being criticized at the time for its promotion of Tokuma productions, and Kanō speculated that this may have contributed to the reduction in marketing.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|pp=102–103}} Ajinomoto created two varieties of branded fruit-flavored sodas featuring illustrations by Miyazaki,{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=102}} and launched a widespread campaign to publicize them beginning in April{{Nbsp}}1986.{{sfn|Denison|2018|pp=40–41}} This included [[sweepstake]]s for branded merchandise{{nbsp}}– among the prizes were [[high fidelity]] sound systems with the film's title, provided by {{nowrap|Toshiba{{sfn|Yoshioka|2018|p=20}} –}} a telephone advertisement service, and a competition to be selected as a "Laputa Reporter" for the [[Osaka]] region.{{sfnm|Denison|2018|1pp=40–41|Kanō|2006|2p=102}} [[File:Sumi Shimamoto at Sakura-Con 2007 Crop (cropped).png|thumb|right|upright=0.7|[[Sumi Shimamoto]] ''(pictured in 2007)'', a lead voice actor from ''[[Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (film)|Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind]]''{{nbsp}}(1984), narrated commercials for this film.{{sfn|Denison|2018|pp=41–42}}|alt=Headshot of Sumi Shimamoto]] Due to Studio Ghibli's restrictions on the footage, the television commercials instead featured a live-action adaptation of the film's elements.{{sfn|Denison|2018|p=41}} A life-size model of a flaptor was created, reportedly at an expense of {{JPY|10 million}} to Ajinomoto, and various specialized equipment was purchased to film it. Two actors were hired to play Pazu and Sheeta, and the narration was provided by Sumi Shimamoto and [[Yōji Matsuda]], the lead voice actors from ''Nausicaä''.{{sfn|Denison|2018|pp=41–42}} The production of these commercials was the subject of significant coverage in ''Animage'', where the challenges and spectacle of the live-action medium were emphasized; the animation scholar [[Rayna Denison]] argued that, inadvertently or not, the campaign became a distraction from the film rather than a supportive accompaniment.{{sfn|Denison|2018|pp=41–42}} However, despite the campaign running during the hot Japanese summer, the drinks did not become particularly popular,{{harvnb|Suzuki|2005|pp=92–93}}, cited in {{harvnb|Denison|2018|p=40}}, and {{harvnb|Yoshioka|2018|p=20}}. only selling around a third of the anticipated 30{{Nbsp}}million bottles.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=102}} The film was additionally promoted with two episodes from ''[[Sherlock Hound]]''{{nbsp}}(1984–1985), a television series Miyazaki had co-directed with {{ill|Kyōsuke Mikuriya|ja|御厨恭輔}}, which would be shown along with the film in theaters.{{efn|The episodes in question were "Mrs. Hudson is Taken Hostage" and "The White Cliffs of Dover".{{sfn|Tomonari|1986|p=54}}}} This was an established tactic at the time, and two other episodes had previously been screened during ''Nausicaä''{{'s}} theatrical run. Denison felt that the more lighthearted episodes were used to compensate for the film's heavier tone, increasing the program's appeal for a general audience. However, unlike with ''Nausicaä'', the episodes in question had already been aired on television.{{sfn|Denison|2018|pp=39–40}} They were also, according to Kanō, of lower animation quality compared with the rest of the series, and held "questionable" potential to attract audiences.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=104}} === Japanese release === A major promotional event was held in [[Shibuya]] on July{{nbsp}}20, 1986, which was attended by key staff and the lead voice actors. The film premiered on July{{nbsp}}25 at the {{ill|Tokyo Chamber of Commerce and Industry|ja|東京商工会議所}}.{{sfnm|Kameyama|2016|1p=12|Kanō|2006|2p=82}} Preview screenings were held over the following week in major Japanese cities with posters put out by the publicity department at the [[Toei Company]], based on illustrations by Miyazaki. These received positive feedback, and the film was publicly recommended by local film societies and children's welfare committees.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=103}} On August{{nbsp}}2, ''Castle in the Sky'' was released by Toei in 103{{nbsp}}theaters around Japan. In its 14-day run in theaters, it attracted 774,271 viewers, earning an estimated {{JPY|1.16 billion}} at the box office and {{JPY|583 million}} from [[distribution rental]]s.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|pp=74, 103}} This was only around two-thirds of the earnings made from ''Nausicaä'', and Miyazaki and Suzuki expressed their disappointment with these figures.{{sfnm|1a1=Denison|1y=2018|1p=43|2a1=Napier|2y=2018|2p=91}} The animation scholar Shiro Yoshioka argued that the restrictions on the marketing were a factor in the film's lower returns.{{sfn|Yoshioka|2018|p=20}} Kanō also wrote that the film's runtime, coupled with the length of the ''Sherlock Hound'' episodes, limited the number of screenings that could take place per day.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=103}} Miyazaki himself attributed the lack of viewership to his defiance of genre expectations and the comparatively unremarkable protagonist.{{harvnb|Kanō|2006|pp=82–83}}, cited in {{harvnb|Napier|2018|p=91}}.{{efn|See {{slink|#Pre-production}} for further information.}} === English dubs === The first English dub was produced by an unknown company in [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood]].{{efn|name=Streamline dub|The company responsible for producing the 1987 dub of ''Castle in the Sky'' is unknown. This dub is sometimes referred to as the "Streamline dub", which led to a misconception that it was produced by [[Streamline Pictures]] themselves.{{sfnm|1a1=Clements|1a2=McCarthy|1y=2015|1p=121|2a1=Patten|2y=2015}} Others attribute the dub to a company called "Magnum".{{sfn|Wyse|2020}} However, the dub was commissioned by [[Tokuma Shoten]] and licensed to Streamline for distribution in North America.{{sfn|Clements|McCarthy|2015|p=121}} [[Fred Patten]], a representative for Streamline, reported that it was originally produced for [[Japan Airlines]] as on-board entertainment on international flights.{{sfn|Toyama}} According to Streamline's co-founder [[Carl Macek]], Tokuma Shoten had outsourced its production to an unnamed company in [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood]].{{harvnb|Macek|2014|loc=48:49–49:17}}: "We didn't dub it. Streamline didn't dub it.{{nbsp}}... It was paid for by Tokuma Shoten, but they just picked some company out in the middle of Hollywood to do it. They just phone-booked the guy." }} It was first screened in Hong{{nbsp}}Kong on June{{nbsp}}26, 1987, with Chinese subtitles,{{sfn|''Nausicaa.net''}} earning around {{HK$|13 million|link=yes}} in three months at the box office.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=105}} It debuted in the United States on July{{nbsp}}14, 1987, at the Los Angeles Animation Celebration.{{sfn|Solomon|1987}} The dub was screened at the [[London Film Festival]] in November, and an edited version briefly aired on television in the United Kingdom.{{efn|name=ITV airing|The 1987 dub was aired by [[ITV (TV network)|ITV]] in some regions of the eastern UK. This airing was altered from the original, with some scenes being cut,{{sfn|Toyama}} and the film being listed on programs as ''Laputa: The Flying Island''.{{sfn|Smithies|1988}} }} The film was licensed for theatrical distribution in North America in 1989 by the then-new [[Streamline Pictures]];{{sfn|Patten|2015}} the release was relatively limited, and its box office earnings are unknown.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=105}} Following the distribution deal struck between Tokuma Shoten and [[Walt Disney Pictures|Disney]] in 1997, which included terms for the dubbing and international release of all Studio Ghibli films, a second English dub was produced. Well-known actors were cast, including [[James Van Der Beek]] (Pazu), [[Anna Paquin]] (Sheeta), and [[Mark Hamill]] (Muska).{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=106}} Due to the possible confusion with the Spanish phrase {{lang|es|la puta}}{{nbsp}}– literally 'the {{nowrap|whore'{{efn|Miyazaki stated that he had not been aware of this meaning during the production, and only later learned that [[Jonathan Swift]] had named [[Laputa|the island]] in ''[[Gulliver's Travels]]''{{nbsp}}(1726) ironically.}} –}} the film was re-titled simply to ''Castle in the Sky''.{{sfn|Greenberg|2018|p=115}} After its completion in 2000, it premiered at the [[New York International Children's Film Festival]] on February{{nbsp}}4.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=106}} However, following the poor performance of ''Princess Mononoke'' in North American theaters, the intended nationwide theatrical release was canceled, and the home media release was postponed.{{sfnm|1a1=Kanō|1y=2006|1p=106|2a1=Wyse|2y=2020}} === Home media and other releases === Following the Japanese theatrical release, Tokuma Shoten released the film on [[VHS]] in August{{nbsp}}1986, and a version on [[LaserDisc]] was released the next month. These sold approximately 80,000 copies over the following three years. A number of books related to the film were published by Studio Ghibli, including an [[Coffee table book#Movies|art book]] and a comic-book version using stills from the film.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=103}} The film gradually gained popularity through subsequent television broadcasts{{nbsp}}– screenings on [[Nippon Television]] from 1988 to 2004 received viewership rates between 12 and {{nowrap|22 percent{{sfn|Kanō|2006|pp=83, 103}} –}} and earned a significant additional amount through re-releases.{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=94}} In Japan, [[Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment|Buena Vista]] reissued the VHS in 1998, which sold around 1{{nbsp}}million copies. Two [[DVD]] collections put out in 2002 sold another 500,000 copies.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=103}} In the United Kingdom, it was the eighth-best-selling foreign language film on home video in 2019.{{sfn|Cade et al.|2020|p=94}} The film has made additional earnings in multiple international theatrical re-runs; it made {{USD|6.6 million}} between 2003 and 2019,{{sfn|''Box Office Mojo''}} and {{USD|19.8 million}} between 2020 and {{As of|2026|bare=yes}}, including at the annual [[Studio Ghibli Fest]].{{sfn|''The Numbers''}} The 2003 English dub was released on DVD in North America on April{{nbsp}}15, 2003.{{sfn|Conrad|2003}} [[Optimum Releasing|Optimum]] released a [[Blu-ray]] version in the United Kingdom in 2011,{{sfn|Vijn|2011}} which Buena Vista brought to North America in 2012;{{sfn|Green|2012}} ''[[The Numbers (website)|The Numbers]]'' estimated the latter earned {{USD|10.3 million}}.{{sfn|''The Numbers''}} After assuming the distribution rights to Studio Ghibli's catalog in North America, [[GKIDS]] re-issued the Blu-rays and DVDs in 2017.{{sfn|Giardina|2017}} Both the original Japanese version and the 2003 English dub were made available for [[streaming]] when the rights to Studio Ghibli's filmography were acquired by [[Netflix]] in 2020.{{sfn|Andrew|2023}} The film was released theatrically in France on January 15, 2003, bringing in 615,374 viewers over the span of a month. The film was subsequently released on DVD there, as well as in Italy and Spain. It had a theatrical and home media release in South Korea in 2004.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=106}} It made its theatrical debut in China on June{{nbsp}}1, 2023,{{sfn|Brzeski|2023}} making {{CNY|76 million|link=yes}} ({{USD|10.7 million}}) in its first week,{{sfn|Frater|2023}} and {{US$|16.5 million}} {{As of|2026|lc=y}}.{{sfn|''The Numbers''}} == Music == [[File:Joe Hisaishi 2011.jpg|thumb|upright=0.7|[[Joe Hisaishi]] ''(pictured in 2011)'', the composer|alt=Joe Hisaishi on stage at a concert]] === Development === [[Joe Hisaishi]], a returning collaborator from ''Nausicaä'', composed ''Castle in the Sky''{{'s}} score. He was not initially planning to fill this role, as he was occupied with composing for ''[[Arion (film)|Arion]]''{{nbsp}}(1986) at the time, but accepted the project at Miyazaki's request.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=98}} The two went on to become close collaborators, and Hisaishi has since written the music for all of Miyazaki's feature films.{{sfn|Napier|2018|p=71}} After he was brought on in February{{nbsp}}1986, Hisaishi began work on the [[image album]], a collection of demos based on the concept materials that serve as a precursor to the finished score.{{sfnm|Bellano|2024|Kameyama|2016|1p=256|2p=12}} Takahata acted as music supervisor,{{sfn|Hara|2024|p=347}} and worked with Hisaishi on a plan for the music required in each scene.{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|1986|p=165}} Each song from the image album was then extended and arranged for full [[symphony orchestra]]; this version was recorded by the {{ill|Tokyo City Philharmonic Orchestra|lt=Tokyo City Philharmonic|ja|東京シティ・フィルハーモニック管弦楽団}}.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=99}} In March, the song {{nihongo foot|"If I Could Fly"|もしも空を飛べたら|Moshimo sora o tobetara|lead=yes|group=lower-alpha}} was commissioned from [[Takashi Matsumoto (lyricist)|Takashi Matsumoto]], who had written a similar song for ''Nausicaä''.{{sfnm|Kameyama|2016|1p=12|Kanō|2006|2p=99}} Unlike the other music, this was not planned to be featured in the film, and only appears in Ajinomoto's television commercials. Kanō described the track, performed by {{ill|Yōko Obata|ja|小幡洋子}}, as similar to other pop music from the time.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=99}} For the final score, Hisaishi aimed to precisely synchronize the music with the on-screen action.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=99}} Advancements in digital playback allowed him to compose while watching the animation to compare their timing; he then sent the pieces to Miyazaki and Takahata for review.{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|1986|p=165}} This resulted in lengthy sequences with uninterrupted background score, and pieces that dynamically switch between different [[Motif (music)|motifs]] to match the scene's point of view.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=99}} While the image album contains prominent electronic elements,{{sfn|Bellano|2010|p=17}} Hisaishi intended for a more "acoustic" sound in the film; the soundtrack version therefore uses [[Fairlight synthesizer]]s alongside a 50-piece orchestra.{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|1986|p=165}} Disagreements between Miyazaki, Takahata, and Hisaishi about which scenes needed background accompaniment led to delays; the music for the opening scene, for example, was written less than a month from the release date.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=99}} {{nihongo foot|"Carrying You"|君をのせて|Kimi o nosete|lead=yes|group=lower-alpha|post=,}} the vocal song that plays over the credits sequence, was requested by Takahata late in the production. He asked Miyazaki to write the lyrics{{nbsp}}– Kanō wrote that they were likely inspired by ''[[Wind, Sand and Stars]]''{{nbsp}}(1939), a memoir by [[Antoine de Saint-Exupéry]]{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=100}}{{nbsp}}– and Hisaishi set them to an arrangement of the film's main theme.{{sfn|Bellano|2010|p=30}} It was performed by [[Azumi Inoue]].{{sfn|''Oricon''}} According to Shigeharu Shiba, ''Castle in the Sky'' was among the first films in Japan to use [[Quadraphonic sound|quadraphonic (4-channel) sound]] for its theatrical release. He avoided using the additional speakers to move sounds around the room{{nbsp}}– as Miyazaki felt the effect became too artificial{{nbsp}}– and instead strove to preserve a "natural sense of space". The final mixing was done at the {{ill|Tokyo Television Center|ja|東京テレビセンター}}. Shiba said that Hisaishi's score required very few changes during the process with the exception of the scene of Laputa's collapse, where Takahata insisted the song be cut off in the middle of the scene.{{sfn|Studio Ghibli|1986|p=164}} === Rewriting for the English dub === [[File:Seattle_Symphony_Orchestra_on_stage_in_Benaroya_Hall_(cropped).jpg|alt=A symphony orchestra on stage|thumb|The soundtrack for the 2003 English dub was performed by the [[Seattle Symphony]] ''(pictured in 2009)''.{{sfn|''Nausicaa.net''|1999}}]] Hisaishi began rewriting the soundtrack for the English dub in March{{Nbsp}}1999, rearranging the original themes in an American cinematic style.{{sfn|Hisaishi|1999}} He was advised by Disney staff that non-Japanese audiences preferred comparatively more music in films. As a result, this soundtrack is much longer, around 90{{Nbsp}}minutes in length, while the Japanese version featured just an hour of music.{{harvnb|''Keyboard''|1999}}, cited in {{harvnb|Osmond|2000}}; {{harvnb|''Nausicaa.net''|1999}}. The new material was used to fill scenes that had previously been silent or partially scored.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=102}} Various other changes were made, and scenes from the original that Miyazaki or Hisaishi had been dissatisfied with were rewritten entirely.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|Studio Ghibli|1986|1pp=101–102|2p=165}} In contrast with the original, he used a "[[Hollywood, Los Angeles|Hollywood]] method", using pieces to directly represent the characters that appear on screen.{{harvnb|Brawley|Thompson|1999}}, cited in {{harvnb|Osmond|2000}}. Although Hisaishi felt that this writing involved an overly simplistic compositional approach, he stated that he "learned a lot" from the experience.{{sfn|''Keyboard''|1999}} As many of the original scores and synthesizer data had been lost by this point, Hisaishi reconstructed them before starting on the adaptation.{{sfn|''Nausicaa.net''|1999}} Every piece in this version was written for symphony orchestra, and many electronic-heavy tracks for the original were rearranged for the ensemble.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=101}} The soundtrack was performed by the [[Seattle Symphony]], which Hisaishi had chosen for their "well-balanced" sound.{{sfn|''Nausicaa.net''|1999}} The recordings took place in [[Seattle]] in late April and early May inside a local church.{{sfnm|1a1=Hisaishi|1y=1999|2a1=''Keyboard''|2y=1999}} === Analysis === The cinema and music scholar Marco Bellano identified the image album as the beginning of a change in Hisaishi's compositional style for Miyazaki's films; it contains more experimental pieces, and the melodies are written with much longer [[Phrase (music)|phrases]].{{sfn|Bellano|2010|p=17}} Hisaishi said that these were drawn from Scottish and Irish folk influences, which often use [[pentatonic scale]]s.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|Studio Ghibli|1986|1p=99|2p=165}} Bellano found that, to match the pacing of the film, these melodies are introduced in their complete forms before being "fragmented" when reappearing in later scenes.{{sfn|Bellano|2010|pp=17–18}} Although Hisaishi uses [[leitmotif]]s{{nbsp}}– short, recurring musical elements tied to aspects of the narrative, such as characters or moods{{nbsp}}– Bellano argued that he developed a novel approach to using leitmotifs due to the particular constraints of composing for a Miyazaki film.{{sfn|Bellano|2010|pp=17–18}} Bellano analyzed the film's main theme as built on a descending four-note line ''(highlighted below in red)'', a technique that would characterize Hisaishi's future melodies in Miyazaki's work:{{sfn|Bellano|2024|p=261}} : { \relative c'' { \language "english" \clef treble \numericTimeSignature \key c \minor \time 4/4 \partial 4 c8 d8 \once \override NoteHead.color = #red ef4 d8 ef8 ~ ef8 g4 \once \override NoteHead.color = #red d8 ~ \once \override NoteHead.color = #red d2. g,4 \once \override NoteHead.color = #red c4 bf8 c8 ~ c8 ef4 \once \override NoteHead.color = #red bf8 ~ \once \override NoteHead.color = #red bf2. } } [[File:Joe Hisaishi - The Girl Who Fell from the Sky (piano excerpt).ogg]] In this film's context, he found the descending pattern reflective of the film's theme of flight; He also praised the ending, in which Sheeta and Pazu choose to leave the island rather than enact a "second [[Adam and Eve]] story".{{harvnb|Yomota|1986}}, republished in {{harvnb|Studio Ghibli|1996|p=118}}, cited in {{harvnb|Kanō|2006|p=106}}. A reviewer for ''{{ill|City Road (magazine)|lt=City Road|ja|シティロード}}'' wrote that the film presents themes that were critical of modern society while still maintaining a "warm and caring" view of humanity.{{harvnb|''City Road''|1986}}, republished in {{harvnb|Studio Ghibli|1996|p=118}}. In ''Kinema Junpo'', Junichi Tomonari was compelled by Pazu's character development from an ordinary boy to someone who "seizes his own future", a choice he felt would leave a considerable impression on audiences.{{sfn|Tomonari|1986|p=55}} Mari Arita of the ''{{ill|Weekly Asahi|ja|週刊朝日}}'' appreciated the film's dynamic action sequences, favorably comparing its flying scenes to those in ''[[Peter Pan (1953 film)|Peter Pan]]''{{nbsp}}(1953). She highlighted the details in the animation,{{harvnb|Arita|1986}}, republished in {{harvnb|Studio Ghibli|Bunshun Bunko|2013|pp=176–178}}. as did the film critic {{ill|Yūkichi Shinada|ja|品田雄吉}} in ''Kinema Junpo'', who also complimented the background art in the first act. He felt, however, that the film did not convincingly blend its Western "[[fairy tale]]" influences and Japanese manga-derived elements.{{sfn|Shinada|1986}} The animator [[Yasuji Mori]] commended the unique atmosphere of the film, but felt it had a "monotonous" pacing, with the many action set pieces rendering the final sequence anticlimactic.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=107}} === Response to the English dubs === On the [[review aggregator]] website [[Metacritic]], the film has a [[weighted average]] score of 78 out of 100 based on seven critics, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.{{sfn|''Metacritic''}} On [[Rotten Tomatoes]], 96% of the 28 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 7.6 out of 10. The website's critical consensus reads, "With a storytelling palette as rich and brilliant as its animation, ''Castle in the Sky'' thrillingly encapsulates Studio Ghibli's unique strengths."{{sfn|''Rotten Tomatoes''}} [[Charles Solomon (animation historian)|Charles Solomon]], writing after the film's 1987 screening in Los Angeles, was highly critical of the film's plot and use of genre clichés.{{sfn|Solomon|1987}} After its London screening, however, a [[Variety (magazine)|''Variety'']] reviewer found the style to be "charming".{{sfn|Adam|1987}} Upon the film's 1989 theatrical release in the United States, Kanō wrote that it received generally negative reviews in the United States.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=105}} While multiple reviewers felt that the film's two-hour According to McCarthy, the film has attained [[Cult film|cult status]] due to its unique blend of themes.{{sfn|McCarthy|2002|p=97}} [[Jeff VanderMeer]] and [[Selena J. Chambers]], in ''[[The Steampunk Bible]]'', included the film among the "first modern steampunk classics."{{sfn|VanderMeer|Chambers|2012|p=183}} Greenberg thought the film was among the greatest in the adventure genre,{{sfn|Greenberg|2018|p=117}} and Murase named it "quite possibly the most entertaining" in Miyazaki's body of work.{{harvnb|Murase|2004|p=82}}, cited in {{harvnb|Napier|2018|p=86}}. ''[[Den of Geek]]''{{'s}} Ryan Lambie felt that Miyazaki's fantasy, including its "utopian, maybe even impossible vision", was convincingly realized.{{sfn|Lambie|2016}} In ''[[The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]]'', Steven Pearce praised the film as an "exciting adventure tale with imaginative, alluring animation, deserving of its high acclaim".{{sfn|Pearce|2021}} Fumiko Tsuneishi also found the animation to be a strength. Writing for a ''Kinema Junpo'' collection on Miyazaki, she compared the film with later entries in Miyazaki's filmography, observing that motifs such as the lead characters' affinity for animals continue to be explored.{{sfn|Tsuneishi|1999|pp=126–129}} Audiences ranked the film third in a poll for the best animated works at the 2006 [[Japan Media Arts Festival]],{{sfnm|1a1=''Agency for Cultural Affairs''|2a1=Macdonald|2y=2006}} and named it the best of all time in a 2008 poll by [[Oricon]].{{sfn|''Oricon''|2008}} In critics' rankings, the film placed 86th on ''[[Time Out (company)|Time Out]]''{{'s}} list of the 100 best animated films,{{sfn|Singer et al.|2025}} and 13th on their list of the 30 best anime.{{sfn|Rothkopf et al.|2026}} It placed 44th on ''Animage''{{'s}} 100 best anime,{{sfn|''Anime News Network''|2001}} and 38th on ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]''{{'s}}.{{sfn|Egan|2024}} === Cultural impact === {{Multiple image | total_width = 305 | perrow = 3 | image1 = Katsura Hoshino Animagic Germany.JPG | image2 = Mamoru Oshii - Lucca Comics & Games 2015.JPG | image3 = MKr26312 Makoto Shinkai (Suzume, Berlinale 2023).jpg | image4 = JohnLasseterOct2011.jpg | image5 = Godzilla Resurgence World Premiere Red Carpet- Anno Hideaki (28526527191) (cropped).jpg | image6 = Chieko Baishō at the Tokyo International Film Festival 2019 (49013476248) (cropped).jpg | footer = ''(Clockwise from top left)'' [[Katsura Hoshino]], [[Mamoru Oshii]], [[Makoto Shinkai]], [[Chieko Baisho]], [[Hideaki Anno]], and [[John Lasseter]]
Several artists have cited ''Castle in the Sky'' as influencial on their work.{{sfnm|Goodman|2011|Kanō|2006|2p=83|Lamarre|2009|3pp=155–156|McCarthy|2002|4p=111|Rose|2016|''Shueisha''|2018}} }} ''Castle in the Sky'' has grown into one of Miyazaki's most internationally well-known creations.{{sfn|Odell|Le Blanc|2015|p=67}} In Japan, a statue of a robot from the film is displayed at the [[Ghibli Museum]],{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=105}} which also hosted an art piece replicating the film's mine carts in 1992{{sfn|Denison|2023|p=127}} and a special exhibition of the production materials in 2002.{{sfn|Kanō|2006|p=105}} Major artists in the anime and manga industries named the film among their favorites, including [[Katsura Hoshino]],{{sfn|''Shueisha''|2018}} [[Mamoru Oshii]],{{sfn|McCarthy|2002|p=111}} and [[Makoto Shinkai]].{{sfn|Rose|2016}} Several of Miyazaki's future collaborators, such as [[Diana Wynne Jones]], [[Yumi Matsutoya]], and [[Chieko Baisho]], developed an appreciation of his work after discovering this film.{{sfnm|Kanō|2006|1p=83|Osmond|2003}} [[Hideaki Anno]], who had previously worked with Miyazaki on the production of ''Nausicaä'',{{sfn|Bricken|2022}} based his series ''[[Nadia: The Secret of Blue Water]]''{{nbsp}}(1990–1991) on one of Miyazaki's concepts dating to the 1970s. Substantial similarities, including the orphaned lead characters, the fantastical nineteenth-century setting, and a powerful pendant, are present as a result.{{sfn|Lamarre|2009|pp=155–156}} [[John Lasseter]], the former [[chief creative officer]] at [[Pixar]], often cited Miyazaki and his works as his "greatest inspiration",{{sfn|Frater|2014}} and named ''Castle in the Sky'' among his favorite Castle in the Sky, also known as Laputa: Castle in the Sky, is a 1986 Japanese animated fantasy adventure film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. It was produced by Isao Takahata, animated by Studio Ghibli, and distributed by the Toei Company. The film stars the voices of Mayumi Tanaka, Keiko Yokozawa, Kotoe Hatsui, and Minori Terada. In the film, orphans Sheeta and Pazu are pursued by government agent Muska, the army, and a group of pirates. They seek Sheeta's crystal necklace, the key to accessing Laputa, a legendary flying castle hosting advanced technology.
Castle in the Sky was the first film to be animated by Studio Ghibli. Its production team included many of Miyazaki's longtime collaborators, who would continue to work with the studio for the following three decades. The film was partly inspired by Miyazaki's trips to Wales, where he witnessed the aftermath of the 1984–1985 coal miners' strike. The island of Laputa is used to highlight the theme of environmentalism, exploring the relationships between humanity, nature, and technology, a reflection of Miyazaki's ecological philosophy. The young protagonists also provide a unique perspective on the narrative, as a result of Miyazaki's desire to portray "the honesty and goodness of children in [his] work". Many aspects of the film's retrofuturistic style – the flying machines in particular – are influenced by nineteenth-century approaches, which has earned the film a reputation in the modern steampunk genre.
The film was released in Japanese theaters on August 2, 1986. It underperformed expectations at the box office, but later achieved commercial success through rereleases. An English dub commissioned by Tokuma Shoten was distributed in North America by Streamline Pictures, and another dub was produced by Disney in 1998, released internationally by Buena Vista in 2003. The film's score was composed by Joe Hisaishi, who would become a close collaborator of Miyazaki's; Hisaishi also composed a reworked soundtrack for the 2003 English dub. The film was generally acclaimed by critics, though the English dubs received mixed reviews. It was well received by audiences, being voted as one of the greatest animated films in polls conducted by the Agency for Cultural Affairs and Oricon. The film also received several notable accolades, including the Ōfuji Noburō Award at the Mainichi Film Awards and the Anime Grand Prix from Animage. Castle in the Sky has since attained cult status, and has influenced several notable artists working in multiple media.
